evidence.title: Fire-Resistant Textile Development for Exploration Vehicles With Enriched-Oxygen Cabin Environments

evidence.text:
National Aeronautics and Space Administration 
2
Background
• Oxygen-enriched cabin exploration atmospheres (>30% O2) are preferred to shorten prebreathing 
time and maximize the duration of EVAs
• The proposed Artemis IV+ atmosphere is 8.2 psia and 34±2% O2 (testing at 37% O2 for contingency)
• Greatly increases flammability risk
Artemis missions planning elevated oxygen cabin environments (>30% O2)
• Selection of fire-resistant textiles is a key part of NASA’s fire prevention strategy to ensure large-
scale flame propagation events do not occur
• Very limited existing Commercial Off-The-Shelf (COTS) textiles can be certified for use in up to 37% 
O2 environments
• Most of the fibers and textiles developed during Apollo (100% O2) and Skylab (70% O2) (i.e., beta 
glass, PBI, Durette, Astro Velcro) that are no longer commercially available due to discontinuation 
of raw materials and closure of the original manufacturers
Significant need for improved non-flammable textiles

evidence.text:
National Aeronautics and Space Administration 
7
Fire-resistant Textile Assessment
• NASA Engineering and Safety Center (NESC) was requested to conduct an 
assessment and develop a strategy for the development of high priority 
fire-resistant textiles for softgoods applications within a vehicle cabin at 
a minimum of 37% O2 at 8.2 psia
• Agency-wide Assessment:
1.
Identify stakeholders and collect data including key performance and safety 
parameters/metrics
2.
Determine material requirements, applications, and NASA program priorities
3.
Comprehensively assess the NASA and industry current state of the art and 
opportunities for fire-resistant textiles
4.
Develop a prioritized strategy and implementation plan

evidence.text:
National Aeronautics and Space Administration 
8
Fire-resistant Textile Strategy
Phase 3
Custom Textile Development
•If no COTS solution can meet NASA-STD-6001B Test 1 and it is not possible to do incremental improvement over COTS solutions, 
a custom major development effort is required with an industrial partner to design and develop a suitable solution that can 
meet NASA’s specific needs
Phase 2
Incremental Improvement over COTS Solutions
•If no COTS solution can meet NASA-STD-6001B Test 1 but a relatively low effort can be done to modify the COTS and increase 
the chance of passing, it is recommended to pursue the incremental improvement/modification on the COTS solution and assess 
the performance again
Phase 1
Baseline Testing of Available COTS Products
•Evaluate and confirm whether COTS materials are available that can be certified for use at 37% O2/8.2 psia for each textile type
•Certification testing will be performed at White Sands Test Facility (WSTF)

package.purpose: Material selection is a key part of the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) spacecraft fire safety management plan. Non-flammable textiles are necessary to ensure large-scale flame propagation events do not occur inside a spacecraft. An increased use of textiles and other softgood material is crucial to the pursuit of exploration spaceflight to reduce mass and volume. Exploration spaceflight missions benefit from enriched oxygen cabin environments (>21% O2) by allowing a reduced prebreathe protocol before Extravehicular Activity (EVA). However, materials become exponentially more flammable the higher the O2 levels become. Recent testing within the agency has revealed the lack of commercial-off-the-shelf (COTS) materials that can meet safety requirements in oxygen-enriched environments. Most of the fibers and textiles developed during Apollo (100% O2 cabin environment) and Skylab (>70% O2 cabin environment) are no longer commercially available due to those Programs ending and the discontinuation of raw materials or closure of the original manufacturers. As NASA returns to higher oxygen concentrations inside spacecraft, non-flammable textile development efforts have begun to meet the agency’s needs. This paper discusses those efforts including overall fire safety approach, state-of-the-art textile review and testing, an agency-wide assessment of textile needs performed by the NASA Engineering and Safety Center (NESC), the textile development strategy and expected challenges.
